title: "I Know It When I See It" Doesn't Scale
author: Molly G.
summary: The piece draws on manager Hilary Gridley's experience building an AI writing-feedback tool for her team to argue that AI's real value for managers isn't automation, it's forcing them to make tacit judgment explicit. Gridley kept giving the same feedback about weak executive emails, but when she tried to instruct an AI to 'make this better,' she discovered she couldn't -- she had to pull together strong and weak examples and distill her unconscious review criteria into explicit principles before the tool could help at all. The author generalizes this into a broader claim about management: many managers act as a bottleneck by inserting themselves as a quality filter on every piece of work rather than teaching people the underlying judgment behind their standards, and AI is now exposing that gap because, unlike a human, it 'refuses to read your mind' and will simply produce mediocre work from vague instructions. The piece closes by reframing the exercise as inherently good management practice regardless of the AI angle: turning tacit intuition into explicit, teachable criteria is what separates managers who create leverage from managers who make themselves the bottleneck.
points: Uses a concrete failure moment -- Gridley unable to tell an AI tool to simply 'make this better' -- to show that AI forces managers to externalize quality criteria they've always applied unconsciously but never had to articulate.

Draws a sharp distinction between filtering and scaling: 'the job of a manager is not to own quality or act as a filter; it is to create leverage,' arguing managers who review every output before it goes out haven't scaled their judgment, they've become the bottleneck.

Frames AI's literalism as a diagnostic feature, not a limitation: humans compensate for vague instructions, AI does not, meaning bad AI output often reveals a pre-existing gap in a manager's own articulated standards.

Generalizes the lesson beyond AI tooling entirely: the discipline of turning 'a presentation feels too long' into explicit, teachable criteria is valuable management practice independent of whether an AI tool is ever built from it.
quotes: Humans are surprisingly good at compensating for vague instructions. Or at least trying to. They fill in gaps. They infer what you probably meant. They learn your preferences over time. AI is much less forgiving.
She couldn't just tell the AI, Make this better. She had to explain what better meant.
The most interesting thing here isn't that she built an AI-writing tool that her team could use; it's that using AI forced her to make something explicit that had always been implicit.
If the only way your team can produce great work is by routing everything through you, then you haven't scaled your judgment. You've just made yourself the bottleneck.

Most of us carry around a lot of tacit knowledge. We know a presentation feels too long or when an email buries the lead or when something isn't quite right. But often, we don't know how to explain why, and no one has ever forced us to.
Ironically, AI may end up making us better managers because it forces us to do something we should have been doing all along: making our judgment visible.
